SECTION 01

Executive Summary

ADIS is an integrated research prototype that evaluates quarterly crop-price forecasts, retrospective sell/store choices, compatible-warehouse allocation, and a single-leg transport-cost proxy. Its quantitative evidence is limited to saved validation folds and stated scenario assumptions.

144valid forecast rows144 expected across 3 crops × 4 models × 3 origins × 4 horizons
144retrospective sell/store casesStandardized 1-quintal scenarios
36warehouse scenariosCBC status: {'Optimal': 36}
36transport proxy scenariosHaversine reference-origin legs; not CVRP
80 passedlatest test run0 failed · 14 warnings · 89.64 seconds (post-generation suite run)

Implementation status: research modules and audits are implemented; repository validation: full test command passed in the recorded run. Forecast selection is procedure-specific. Storage, spoilage, warehouse rates, and transport are scenario assumptions. There is no causal farmer-income evaluation.

AI disclosure: a separate chatbot client is configured for a local OpenAI-compatible LLM service; it is not the forecasting, optimization, or statistical-validation engine.

SECTION 02

Dataset & Data Pipeline

The forecast source is quarterly and uses the explicitly labeled Price_INR_per_Quintal field. Crop-wise duplicate quarters are averaged; missing source prices and calendar gaps are not interpolated. The evaluation uses the longest contiguous segments: Rice 26 observations (2009Q1-2015Q2), Onion 26 (2009Q1-2015Q2), Tomato 24 (2009Q3-2015Q2; 2009Q2 gap excluded).

Farmer-study description provided for this report: 150 farmers in Tirunelveli region including Tenkasi; January-March 2026; direct/local farming-network recruitment; consent obtained; crop name, cultivated area, cultivation season; three crops per farmer; 450 farmer-crop observations. The supplied CSV has 450 rows and fields Serial_No, Farmer_ID, Crop_Cultivated, Crop_Yield_tonnes_per_acre, Season; it does not itself encode recruitment dates, consent, area, or region. These study descriptors therefore remain report-level documentation rather than fields independently verifiable from that CSV.

The farmer dataset has 450 rows and 150 distinct farmer IDs where the ID field is present; each crop has 150 rows. This count does not by itself establish that farmer-level yield or income outcomes were used in the forecasting/decision evaluation. The warehouse source contains no observed farmer origin, carrier tariff provenance, or actual billing period.

Forecast split: no random split or separately held test set is used in the validated forecast experiment. The latest three non-overlapping rolling origins are used chronologically, expanding training from 12 to 16 to 20 observations and validating four following quarters at each origin. Gaps are excluded rather than filled.

SECTION 03

System Architecture

Research computation is separate from the farmer-facing conversational UI. Forecast rows are saved before sell/store scoring; warehouse allocation consumes selected-model decision scenarios; routing consumes warehouse allocations. Robustness audits consume those saved artifacts.

Implemented: crop-wise preprocessing, rolling-origin forecast models, formula-based retrospective sell/store, cost-minimizing continuous warehouse allocation, and deterministic artifact audits.
Scenario-based: one-quintal decisions, assumed storage/spoilage costs, warehouse cost rates, synthetic origin, Haversine transport, sensitivity multipliers.
Limited / unsupported: calibrated probabilistic uncertainty for every model, causal farmer welfare, actual farmer routing, road-network routing, and genuine CVRP.
SECTION 04

Forecasting Models

All models receive only the training prefix for their fold. Metrics compare each complete four-quarter validation vector with aligned actual prices. LSTM scaling is fit on training data per fold; forecast outputs are generated recursively.

ModelMethodInput / trainingValidation / roleLimitations
Seasonal NaiveRepeats the final four training observations in sequence: y-hat(t+h)=y(t-4+((h-1) mod 4)).Observed crop-specific quarterly price series; no fitted parameters.Evaluated on the same three rolling origins; comparison baseline, not selected as current crop choice.Seasonal cycle only; no probabilistic interval.
ARIMASARIMAX implementation with order (1,1,1), no seasonal terms.Each expanding training fold; stationarity and invertibility enforced; L-BFGS, max 500 iterations.4-step fold forecasts; eligible for model selection and native 95% intervals.Small number of origins; convergence/initialization warnings recorded.
SARIMASARIMAX with (p,d,q)=(0,1,1), seasonal (P,D,Q,s)=(0,1,1,4).Each expanding training fold; stationarity and invertibility enforced; L-BFGS, max 500 iterations.4-step fold forecasts; eligible for selection and native 95% intervals.Seasonal parameters estimated from short series; small-sample warnings.
LSTMInput(window,1) -> LSTM(32, ReLU) -> Dense(1); recursive multi-step predictions.Train-fold MinMax scaling; lookback min(4, n_train-1); Adam 0.001, MSE, 20 epochs, batch 8, no shuffle; seed 42.Refit within each fold; evaluated against statistical baselines.Only 8, 12, and 16 supervised sequences per fold; no calibrated native interval.

ARIMA/SARIMA form: the implementation estimates a SARIMAX model, which can be written as phi(B) Phi(B^4) (1-B)^d (1-B^4)^D y_t = c + theta(B) Theta(B^4) epsilon_t; for ARIMA the seasonal polynomial terms are identity, and for SARIMA the configured orders are applied. This is a model-family representation; fitted coefficients vary by crop and fold.

LSTM recurrence: standard gated recurrent state updates are trained on scaled supervised windows; exact trained weights are fold-specific and not presented as fixed paper constants.

For decision evaluation, raw lower, point, and upper forecasts are retained in parallel with evaluation values clamped to zero. This follows the decision function’s nonnegative-price constraint. The clamp changes only sensitivity evaluation inputs; it does not alter saved forecasts.

Forecast-error propagation and interval decision robustness are deterministic scenario checks. They do not establish a calibrated predictive distribution or probabilistic farmer outcome.

SECTION 08

Sell-vs-Store Decision Model

Sell now valueV_sell = Q × P0
Stored quantityQ_store = Q × (1 - spoilage)
Storage costC_storage = (Q quintals × 100 kg/quintal) × rate (INR/kg/month) × duration (months)
Store valueV_store = Q_store × P_forecast - C_storage - transport_cost
ActionStore if V_store > V_sell; otherwise Sell

The decision function uses the point forecast and does not receive future actual prices. Ties resolve to Sell because the code uses a strict greater-than comparison. Retrospective actual prices are used only after choosing the action, to score decision agreement and regret.

  • Scenario quantity: 1.00 quintal.
  • Storage rate (INR/kg/month): {"Onion": 0.55, "Rice": 0.3, "Tomato": 0.6}.
  • Spoilage applied once per holding decision: {"Onion": 0.08, "Rice": 0.01, "Tomato": 0.15}.
  • Duration: 3.00 months per forecast quarter, multiplied by horizon.
  • Transport in this decision phase: 0.00 INR scenario charge, configured as zero because no validated route-specific quote is available.

Assumptions are scenario parameters, not measured farm invoices or validated post-harvest-loss observations.

SECTION 10

Forecast Error Sensitivity

Scenario-based forecast-error sensitivity analysis. The audit uses observed absolute forecast errors to perturb forecast-dependent values through the implemented sell/store decision rule. Propagated value error equals absolute forecast error × effective stored quantity after spoilage. It is deterministic, not a probability distribution.

Configured forecast perturbations for the end-to-end scenarios: -20%, -15%, -10%, -5%, 0%, +5%, +10%, +15%, +20%. The existing phase sensitivity file contains 48 rows; the propagated audit file contains 48 crop/model/horizon groups.

SECTION 11

End-to-End Parameter Sensitivity

The output covers 3,456 one-factor-at-a-time decision scenarios over forecast error, storage cost, spoilage, transport cost, and quantity. Warehouse and routing costs are filled only when matching selected-model layer scenarios exist in the saved sensitivity artifacts; 396 warehouse and 252 routing layer rows are supported, with 252 combined totals. Other layer fields remain blank with a status reason, rather than carrying forward baseline cost.

Patterns are descriptive of these configured scenarios only. Quantity and transport changes can scale downstream proxy costs; transport changes do not flip sell/store actions under the phase assumption where decision transport cost is zero. This is not a causal analysis.

SECTION 12

Warehouse Allocation

Formulation correction: the project labels this stage “MILP”, but its decision variables are continuous divisible quantities with no integer/binary restrictions. The saved implementation is mathematically a linear program solved through PuLP CBC, not a mixed-integer model.

Decision variablesx[c,w] ≥ 0; u[c] ≥ 0
Objectivemin Σ x[c,w](storage_cost[c,w] + transport_cost[c,w]) + u[c] × shortage_penalty
Quantity balanceΣ compatible_w x[c,w] + u[c] = available_quantity[c]
Capacityx[c,w] ≤ compatible_capacity[w]

Compatible facilities are selected by crop-support flags. Capacity converts MT × 10 to quintals. Storage source rates are treated as INR/MT/month and converted to INR/quintal/month; transport is configured at INR 5.00/km/MT. The unallocated penalty is INR 1,000,000.00/quintal in the solver objective, but is excluded from reported storage-plus-transport total cost.

SECTION 13

Transport-Cost Evaluation Using Haversine Reference-Origin Proxy

This section is Transport-Cost Evaluation Using Haversine Reference-Origin Proxy. The origin is the arithmetic centroid of warehouse coordinates, not a farmer/customer coordinate; each assigned warehouse is a destination. Distances are straight-line spherical distances using Earth radius 6,371 km. The implementation does not construct vehicle tours or road routes.

Origin centroid recorded in routing validation: latitude 10.872450, longitude 77.896333. Transport cost = distance_km × allocated_quintals / 10 × configured INR 5.00/km/MT.

SECTION 20

LLM / AI Development Disclosure

Generative AI / LLM Usage

The project is reported as using a local LLM through LM Studio for conversational agricultural assistance. The repository chatbot client is configured with the model tag llama-3.2-3b-instruct and a local-network OpenAI-compatible endpoint at 192.168.31.36:1234. The exact served model build/revision and LM Studio runtime identity are not recorded in the current technical artifacts.

Deterministic research pipeline
Forecasting, statistical metrics, sell/store equations, warehouse LP, transport proxy, and artifact audits are implemented in Python/statistical/optimization code. The LLM is not used as the forecasting model, optimizer, or validation engine.
Local LLM-assisted functionality
Conversational responses in the chatbot path only. The local service is separate from saved experimental outputs and does not produce the reported CSV metrics.
Human/developer oversight
Forecast choices and scenario outputs are research evidence subject to review; final decisions remain with users. No automated LLM-generated experimental results are documented.

Source review also finds duplicate chat method definitions in the chatbot class; the later API-backed definition overrides the earlier trained-model branch. This report therefore describes the effective configured client path, not an independently verified locally trained model.

SECTION 21

Limitations

Interpretation boundary

Evidence supports software behavior and configured retrospective/scenario calculations. It does not establish field effectiveness, farmer-income improvement, operational cost savings, or generalizable forecasting superiority.

  1. Only three rolling-origin validation origins are available; DM comparisons do not support significance or superiority conclusions.
  2. The labeled crop-price series is quarterly and short; it does not provide broad market, geographic, or daily variation.
  3. LSTM has a small effective training sample of 8, 12, and 16 sequences per fold.
  4. Forecast-error propagation is deterministic sensitivity analysis, not calibrated probabilistic uncertainty.
  5. Storage, spoilage, quantity, and duration are scenario assumptions; measured farmer invoices and validated post-harvest loss observations are unavailable.
  6. Warehouse dataset provenance is unverified; source storage currency and billing period are unspecified. Transport rates are assumptions, not carrier quotes.
  7. The warehouse formulation has continuous allocation variables and is an LP despite project use of the MILP label.
  8. Transport is a single-leg Haversine reference-origin proxy, not a road route or CVRP. No farmer origin, customer/market demand, vehicle fleet/capacity, travel time, or route logs are available.
  9. No causal farmer-income evaluation or validated farmer-level post-harvest-loss measurement is present.
  10. Model selection is specific to the configured rolling-origin procedure and does not establish universal model superiority.
  11. The local LLM is a separate conversational feature and is not the statistical or optimization engine; exact served model revision is not documented.
  12. The project-provided farmer study description is not fully represented as fields in the supplied farmer CSV, limiting independent row-level verification.

SECTION 24

Final Technical Conclusion

The repository contains an implemented, tested decision-support research pipeline comprising crop-wise quarterly forecasting, rolling-origin evaluation, retrospective sell/store scoring, continuous cost-minimizing warehouse allocation, single-leg Haversine transport-cost scenarios, and artifact-grounded robustness checks. The current outputs have been evaluated and validated under the implemented experimental design, subject to the documented small-sample, provenance, assumption, and routing limitations.

The evidence supports transparent decision analysis and software validation. It does not prove model superiority, guarantee higher farmer profit, establish real-world routing savings, solve CVRP, or demonstrate elimination of post-harvest losses.

TECHNICAL STATUS: VALIDATED WITH LIMITATIONSRetrospective and scenario-based evidence only; human interpretation remains necessary.
